Hyperlipidemia is a prevalent metabolic disorder characterized by elevated levels of lipids in the blood, resulting from a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors such as unhealthy diet and sedentary lifestyle ( 2 ). It is a significant contributor to the global burden of cardiovascular diseases, with studies estimating that over 50% of adults in the United States exhibit elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels ( 3 ). This condition is strongly associated with the development of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), significantly increasing the risk of ASCVD ( 4 ). Beyond ASCVD, hyperlipidemia also contributes to other complications such as pancreatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and metabolic syndrome, further underscoring the need for effective management ( 5 – 8 ). Currently, the treatment of hyperlipidemia primarily relies on statins, especially high-intensity statins (such as atorvastatin and rosuvastatin), which are the first-line treatment due to their excellent effect in lowering LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) and reducing cardiovascular events ( 9 ). However, despite the effectiveness of high-intensity statins in most patients, some individuals fail to achieve optimal LDL-C levels, a phenomenon referred to as the “residual risk after statin therapy” ( 10 ). Additionally, some patients cannot tolerate high-dose statins due to statin intolerance or side effects. These clinical challenges have prompted researchers and clinicians to explore additional lipid-lowering agents that can be used in combination with statins to further optimize lipid control. Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors are a new class of lipid-lowering drugs. By inhibiting CETP activity, they prevent the transfer of cholesterol from high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) to other lipoproteins, thereby raising HDL-C levels and lowering LDL-C levels ( 11 , 12 ). This mechanism offers a potential adjunctive treatment option for hyperlipidemic patients, particularly those who are unresponsive to or intolerant of statin therapy. However, despite the favorable lipid-lowering effects observed in early studies, CETP inhibitors may increase mortality and cardiovascular disease risks ( 13 ). Based on current research, there is growing evidence supporting combination lipid-lowering strategies to optimally reduce lipid levels ( 14 ) he combination of high-intensity statins and CETP inhibitors has garnered widespread attention and is considered a potential comprehensive lipid management option for hyperlipidemic patients. Nevertheless, a systematic review of the combined effects of high-intensity statins and CETP inhibitors on lipid metabolism is still lacking. Therefore, this study aims to synthesize the available data through a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of combined therapy with high-intensity statins and CETP inhibitors on lipid levels in patients. By performing a comprehensive analysis of these study results, it aims to provide more reliable evidence to guide clinical practice and help physicians make more informed decisions when developing individualized treatment plans for hyperlipidemic patients. 2 Methods This study follows the guidelines of the 2015 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement ( 15 ). The protocol for our review was registered in PROSPERO under the registration number CRD42024581470. Ethical approval and patient consent were not required for this study. 2.1 Literature search and selection Two independent researchers performed a systematic search of the PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science databases, covering studies from the databases’ inception until May 9, 2024. The search strategies were adapted for each database, using MeSH terms “Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors” and “Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins” along with relevant free-text terms. Boolean operators “OR” and “AND” were applied to build the search queries (details of the search strategy can be found in the appendix). In addition, we reviewed the reference lists of the retrieved studies to identify other relevant articles. Two researchers (XLB and WH) independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of the initially identified studies. Studies were included if they met the following criteria (1): randomized controlled trials or crossover trials involving human participants; (2) published in English; (3) the intervention group received combination therapy with high-intensity statins and cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors, while the control group received either placebo or monotherapy; (4) studies included at least one of the following outcomes: high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), apolipoprotein AI (ApoAI), apolipoprotein B (ApoB), and adverse events. Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (1) the type or dose of the drugs used was not clearly specified; (2) complete outcome data were not available; (3) they were letters, editorials, case reports, conference abstracts, meta-analyses, reviews, or patents. According to the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines ( 16 ), high-intensity statins were defined as daily doses of 20 or 40 mg of rosuvastatin or 40–80 mg of atorvastatin. 2.2 Quality assessment The methodological quality of all included studies was independently evaluated by two researchers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool RoB 2.0. The assessment focused on five key domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in outcome measurement, and bias in selective outcome reporting. 2.3 Data extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two researchers (XLB and WH). Discrepancies were resolved through discussion with a third researcher until consensus was reached. The following information was extracted from the full texts of the included studies: basic information (first author, year of publication, country of study, study design), study cohort information (sample size, age, treatment drugs, dosage, follow-up duration), and outcome measures. The primary outcome measures included: (1) HDL-C; (2) LDL-C. Secondary outcome measures were: (1) TC; (2) TG; (3) ApoAI; (4) ApoB; (5) adverse events. 2.4 Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using STATA 16.0. In studies with more than one intervention group, the control group was split between the two intervention groups to avoid double-counting in the meta-analysis. For continuous variables, normally distributed data were presented as mean ± standard deviation, while non-normally distributed data were presented as median (interquartile range). We calculated the standardized mean difference (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for HDL-C, LDL-C, TC, TG, ApoAI, and ApoB. For dichotomous variables, we calculated the risk ratio (RR) and 95% CIs for adverse events. To assess heterogeneity between studies, we used the chi-squared test and the I² statistic. I² values of 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75% were interpreted as no heterogeneity, low heterogeneity, moderate heterogeneity, and high heterogeneity, respectively. A fixed-effects model was used if I² was <50% and clinical and methodological heterogeneity among studies was minimal; otherwise, a random-effects model was applied. Furthermore, to investigate the sources of heterogeneity and ascertain the relationship between the types of CETP inhibitors and lipid-lowering effects, we conducted a subgroup analysis based on the categories of CETP inhibitors. All meta-analysis results were displayed in forest plots. Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test and a visual inspection of funnel plots. Additionally, we performed sensitivity analysis using a “leave-one-out” method to assess the robustness of the results by comparing meta-analyses including all studies with those after removing one study at a time. 3 Results 3.1 Search results and study selection The flowchart for the literature search and screening process is shown in Figure 1 . A total of 2,552 relevant records were identified from the following databases: PubMed (n = 471), Embase (n = 1,440), Cochrane Library (n = 119), and Web of Science (n = 522). After removing duplicate articles, 1,730 articles were screened based on their titles and abstracts. We limited the language of the articles to English, resulting in the exclusion of 76 articles. Additionally, 1,254 articles were excluded due to inappropriate article types. Another 140 articles were excluded because their studies were conducted on animals or cells. Moreover, 199 articles were excluded as their interventions were not relevant to this study. Figure 1 Literature search and screening flowchart. Subsequently, we conducted a full-text review and screening of 61 articles, excluding 54 of them. Ultimately, 7 articles were included in the study ( 17 – 23 ). Among the excluded articles, 30 did not meet the definition of high-intensity statin interventions, and 24 either lacked relevant outcomes or had incomplete data. The main characteristics of the included studies are presented in Supplementary Material ( Supplementary Table 2 ). 3.2 Risk of bias The risk of bias for the 7 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool, RoB 2.0. Among the included studies, there were 5 randomized controlled trials and 2 crossover trials. The proportion of risk of bias and the overall methodological quality assessment are shown in Figures 2 and 3 . Of these, 3 studies were of high quality, with all five domains assessed by the risk
assessment tool rated as low risk. However, the study by Nicholls et al. ( 22 ) did not provide a description of the outcome measurement methods, leading to a high rivsk of bias for outcome measurement. Overall, the quality of the included studies was high. Figure 2 Proportion of risk of bias. Figure 3 Overall methodological quality assessment. 3.3 Meta-analysis results 3.3.1 HDL-C Six studies investigated the effect of combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors on HDL-C, including 5,575 participants (2,838 in the experimental group and 2,737 in the control group). The results showed that the combination therapy significantly increased HDL-C levels (SMD 2.47 [1.77, 3.18], I² = 98.4%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 4 ). Figure 4 Forest plot for HDL-C. 3.3.2 LDL-C Six studies also examined the effect of high-intensity statins combined with CETP inhibitors on LDL-C, with 5,556 participants (2,829 in the experimental group and 2,727 in the control group). The results indicated that LDL-C levels were significantly reduced in the experimental group compared to the control group (SMD -1.75 [-2.19, -1.31], I² = 96.9%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 5 ). Figure 5 Forest plot for LDL-C. 3.3.3 Total cholesterol Three studies investigated the effect of combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors on TC, involving 964 participants (480 in the experimental group and 484 in the control group). The pooled analysis showed no statistically significant difference in TC changes between the experimental and control groups (SMD -0.70 [-1.58, 0.18], I² = 92.5%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 6 ). Figure 6 Forest plot for TC. 3.3.4 Triglycerides Five studies examined the effect of the combination therapy on TG. The results indicated that TG levels significantly decreased in the combination therapy group compared to the control group (SMD -0.75 [-1.34, -0.16], I² = 92.3%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 7 ). Figure 7 Forest plot for TG. 3.3.5 ApoAI Five studies explored the effect of combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors on ApoAI levels. The results showed that ApoAI levels in the experimental group significantly increased (SMD 1.99 [1.39, 2.59], I² = 92.3%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 8 ). Figure 8 Forest plot for ApoAI. 3.3.6 ApoB Four studies investigated the effect of the combination therapy on ApoB levels, with the results indicating a significant reduction in ApoB levels in the experimental group (SMD -2.12 [-2.72, -1.52], I² = 97.3%, p < 0.001) ( Figure 9 ). Figure 9 Forest plot for ApoB. 3.3.7 Adverse reactions Five studies reported the occurrence of adverse reactions in both the experimental and control groups. The pooled results showed no statistically significant difference in the risk of adverse reactions between the combination therapy and statin monotherapy (RR 0.88 [0.60, 1.28], I² = 67.3%, p = 0.009) ( Figure 10 ). Figure 10 Forest plot for AEs. 3.4 Subgroup analysis To determine the relationship between different types of CETP inhibitors and lipid-lowering effects, a subgroup analysis was conducted on the included studies. Based on the type of CETP inhibitor used in the combination therapy, the studies were categorized into the “torcetrapib” group, “dalcetrapib” group, “evacetrapib” group, and “obicetrapib” group. The results showed that the “dalcetrapib” group did not demonstrate a significant difference in HDL-C elevation compared to the control group (SMD 0.55 [-0.61, 1.71], I² = 89.0%, p = 0.003) ( Figure 11 ). However, other types of CETP inhibitors combined with high-intensity statins significantly increased HDL-C levels in the participants. Figure 11 Subgroup analysis for HDL-C. On the other hand, all types of CETP inhibitors combined with high-intensity statins significantly reduced LDL-C levels in participants. Among them, “obicetrapib” had the most pronounced effect in lowering LDL-C levels (SMD -10.28 [-12.07, -8.48], I² = 40.4%, p = 0.195) ( Figure 12 ), while there was no significant difference between the “torcetrapib,” “dalcetrapib,” and “evacetrapib” groups. Figure 12 Subgroup analysis for LDL-C. 3.5 Publication bias and sensitivity analysis To assess publication bias for the outcome indicators in the included studies, funnel plots were used for visual representation, and Egger’s test was applied for further analysis. A P-value > 0.05 was considered indicative of no publication bias. The results indicated no publication bias for HDL-C (P = 0.963) and LDL-C (P = 0.155) ( Figures 13 , 14 ). Figure 13 Funnel plot for HDL-C. Figure 14 Funnel plot for LDL-C. For the sensitivity analysis, each study was systematically excluded one by one, and the remaining studies were reanalyzed to determine whether any single study had an excessive impact on the results. The sensitivity analysis showed that no single study excessively influenced the overall results, confirming that the meta-analysis results were stable and reliable. 4 Discussion This study evaluated the lipid-modulating effects of combining CETP inhibitors with high-intensity statins, with particular focus on changes in HDL-C and LDL-C levels. LDL-C is typically considered the primary target for intervention in patients with hypercholesterolemia ( 24 ). Statins are the first-line therapy for lowering LDL-C, but their use, whether as monotherapy or in combination with other lipid-lowering agents, has not been fully optimized. For patients requiring further LDL-C reduction to reach their therapeutic goals, statin monotherapy is often insufficient. Consequently, there is a pressing need for additional lipid-lowering therapies for many patients whose LDL-C levels exceed ideal standards. Cholesterol in plasma primarily exists in the form of cholesterol esters. CETP, a plasma glycoprotein secreted by the liver, is present in humans, non-human primates, and certain other animals. It facilitates the transfer of cholesterol esters and triglycerides between HDL, VLDL, and LDL particles ( 25 ). CETP activity typically facilitates the transfer of cholesterol esters from HDL to VLDL and LDL, while triglycerides are transferred from VLDL to LDL and HDL ( 26 ). CETP inhibition disrupts the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apoB-containing lipoproteins, augments transintestinal cholesterol excretion, upregulates the expression of scavenger receptor class B type 1 and hepatic LDL receptors, and enhances the catabolic efficiency of both LDL particles and apoB ( 27 ). When used in combination with statins, statins reduce intracellular cholesterol levels by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, thereby upregulating LDL receptor expression and enhancing the clearance of LDL particles from the circulation ( 28 ). CETP inhibitors complement this mechanism by increasing HDL-C levels and reducing LDL-C levels, which further stimulates LDL receptor expression ( 29 ). Early clinical trials demonstrated encouraging outcomes in patients with dyslipidemia treated with CETP inhibitors ( 30 – 33 ), but the development of these inhibitors encountered several disappointing challenges in later-stage trials. The first CETP inhibitor evaluated in phase 3 clinical trials was torcetrapib, but the trial results revealed an increased risk of cardiovascular events and death, leading to the premature termination of the trial and cessation of torcetrapib’s development ( 13 ). Dalcetrapib had relatively modest effects, raising HDL-C levels, but its cardioprotective effects were not significant in the phase 3 dal-OUTCOMES trial, resulting in the termination of the project in 2012 ( 34 ). However, dalcetrapib may be effective in patients with specific genotypes, such as variations in the ADCY9 gene, and related research is ongoing. Evacetrapib showed promising results in raising HDL-C and lowering LDL-C in early trials, but the phase 3 ACCELERATE trial failed to demonstrate a significant reduction in cardiovascular events, leading to the discontinuation of the project in 2015 ( 35 ). Due to the premature termination of these clinical trials, significant gaps remain in our understanding. The mechanisms of adverse reactions observed in the later stages of the trials have not been fully elucidated. For example, the excess mortality associated with torcetrapib has been linked to off-target drug effects related to its unique structure ( 13 ), but the reasons for the electrolyte imbalance are still under question. Moreover, the early discontinuation of these trials has left us without long-term data on both efficacy and safety. Over time, such studies could have provided critical insights into the sustainability of treatment benefits and the potential for delayed adverse effects ( 36 ). Despite these past challenges, current research is increasingly focused on the potential of CETP inhibitors to reduce cardiovascular risk by lowering LDL-C levels. Obicetrapib, an oral, once-daily, low-dose CETP inhibitor, is still under development. It has shown promise not only in treating dyslipidemia and lowering cardiovascular risk but also in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease ( 37 ). Regarding lipid modulation, it effectively lowers LDL-C, non-HDL-C, ApoB, and LDL particle concentrations, particularly small LDL particles and lipoprotein(a), while raising mature HDL particles and ApoAI levels ( 38 – 41 ). These findings align with our meta-analysis results. In Nicholls et al.’s study ( 16 ), the experimental group treated with obicetrapib combined with high-intensity statins demonstrated superior efficacy in raising HDL-C and ApoAI and lowering LDL-C and ApoB compared to other CETP inhibitors combined with statins. This suggests that obicetrapib holds potential for helping patients who have not reached their LDL-C goals, filling a gap in current therapies ( 42 ). Another critical aspect of CETP inhibitors is their ability to lower ApoB. A study found that torcetrapib lowers VLDL, IDL, LDL, and ApoB levels primarily by increasing the clearance of ApoB100, while in combination with atorvastatin, torcetrapib reduces ApoB levels by enhancing VLDL ApoB100 clearance and decreasing IDL and LDL ApoB100 production ( 43 ). This study also showed that combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors significantly reduced ApoB, indicating that obicetrapib may currently be the most effective CETP inhibitor for lowering both LDL-C and ApoB, particularly when combined with high-intensity statins. Regarding safety, the Nicholls et al. study ( 22 ) did not report any significant differences in adverse events or off-target effects with obicetrapib. Similarly, this meta-analysis showed that combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors did not increase adverse event rates. Furthermore, Harada et al. ( 44 ) found in their clinical study in Japan that the safety profile of obicetrapib as an adjunct to statin therapy was not influenced by racial differences. This also provides evidence for the potential safety of using this more potent CETP inhibitor either alone or in combination. Our meta-analysis has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, the included studies exhibited significant heterogeneity, particularly in HDL-C and LDL-C outcomes, with I² values of 98.4% and 96.9%, respectively. This substantial heterogeneity may stem from variations in study design, patient populations, or the types of CETP inhibitors used. Although subgroup analysis by CETP inhibitor type did not fully resolve this issue, it highlights the complexity of interpreting pooled results. Additionally, some of the included studies employed cross-sectional designs, which limit the ability to draw causal conclusions. While these studies provide valuable insights into the association between statins, CETP inhibitors, and lipid-lowering effects, they cannot confirm a direct causal relationship. Future longitudinal studies are needed to establish whether the observed benefits are directly attributable to the combination therapy. Furthermore, due to our stringent restriction on the daily dose of statin therapy, the relatively small sample sizes of some included studies may limit the statistical power and generalizability of our findings. Another limitation is the potential for bias in some studies due to insufficient reporting of outcome measurement methods. It has been noted that the indirect measurement of LDL-C using the Friedewald equation may underestimate true levels, potentially exaggerating the effects of CETP inhibitors, while the beta-quantification method, a more accurate approach, has not been widely adopted ( 45 , 46 ). This may introduce variability in the interpretation of lipid-lowering effects and safety outcomes. Future studies should strive for standardized measurement protocols and transparent reporting to enhance the reliability of findings. Finally, existing research has shown that combining obicetrapib with ezetimibe, in addition to high-intensity statin therapy, can significantly reduce atherogenic lipid and lipoprotein parameters while maintaining good safety and tolerability ( 38 ). Although we did not include studies investigating triple-drug combinations, it is important to recognize the potential of these combination therapies, such as CETP inhibitors used alongside ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors in conjunction with high-intensity statins. These combinations may further reduce LDL-C and other atherogenic lipid parameters, offering a more comprehensive approach to lipid management. Despite the less-than-ideal results of CETP inhibitors in early clinical trials, recent studies highlight their potential in reducing LDL-C levels and cardiovascular risk. Obicetrapib, a new CETP inhibitor, has demonstrated significant lipid-lowering effects and good safety profiles when used alongside statin therapy. While the effects of different CETP inhibitors vary, and evidence for the combination of CETP inhibitors with high-intensity statins has been lacking, this meta-analysis fills this gap. However, to further strengthen the evidence base for personalized lipid-lowering strategies and improve cardiovascular disease prevention, future large-scale, multi-center randomized controlled trials are needed. These studies should focus on long-term follow-up to comprehensively evaluate the safety and efficacy of CETP inhibitors in combination with high-intensity statins, particularly in diverse patient populations and under varying clinical conditions. 5 Conclusion This meta-analysis demonstrates that combining high-intensity statins with CETP inhibitors significantly increases HDL-C and reduces LDL-C, TG, and ApoB levels without increasing adverse events. Obicetrapib showed the most pronounced lipid-lowering effects, while dalcetrapib had limited HDL-C elevation. Despite high heterogeneity and small sample sizes in some studies, these findings suggest that combination therapy, particularly with obicetrapib, may benefit patients not achieving optimal lipid control with statin monotherapy. Further large-scale trials are needed to confirm long-term efficacy and safety. documents.title: The impact of very-low-calorie ketogenic diets on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze the effects of very-low-calorie ketogenic diets (VLCKD) on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity.
METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across four electronic databases-PubMed, EBSCOhost, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science-up to June 2025. Outcomes included changes in gut microbial diversity and the relative abundance of key taxa. Subgroup analyses were performed based on body mass index (BMI), age, and intervention duration.
RESULTS: A total of 14 studies were included. Random-effects meta-analysis revealed that VLCKD interventions significantly improved gut microbial α-diversity, as indicated by increased Shannon index (SMD: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.03 to 1.04, P = 0.0378) and Faith's Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) index (SMD: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.36 to 1.18, P = 0.0002). In addition, VLCKD significantly increased the abundance of Akkermansia (SMD: 1.76, 95% CI: 0.48 to 3.03, P = 0.0069) and the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio (SMD: 1.01, 95% CI: 0.67 to 1.34, P SMD: -1.23, 95% CI: -1.81 to -0.64, P 30 years. Akkermansia showed a greater increase in those with BMI 30-35 kg/m², age >40 years, and intervention duration ≤6 weeks. Conversely, Bifidobacterium abundance declined significantly in individuals with BMI 30-35 kg/m², age >40 years, and within an intervention period ≤12 weeks.
CONCLUSION: VLCKD appears to be a promising dietary intervention for modulating gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. However, its bidirectional effects on microbial ecology warrant caution. Future studies should further investigate its long-term safety and explore personalized strategies for microbiota-targeted interventions.
documents.conclusions: VLCKD appears to be a promising dietary intervention for modulating gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. However, its bidirectional effects on microbial ecology warrant caution. Future studies should further investigate its long-term safety and explore personalized strategies for microbiota-targeted interventions.

ABSTRACT Objective This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze the effects of very-low-calorie ketogenic diets (VLCKD) on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. Methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted across four electronic databases—PubMed, EBSCOhost, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science—up to June 2025. Outcomes included changes in gut microbial diversity and the relative abundance of key taxa. Subgroup analyses were performed based on body mass index (BMI), age, and intervention duration. Results A total of 14 studies were included. Random-effects meta-analysis revealed that VLCKD interventions significantly improved gut microbial α -diversity, as indicated by increased Shannon index ( SMD : 0.54, 95% CI : 0.03 to 1.04, P = 0.0378) and Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) index ( SMD : 0.77, 95% CI : 0.36 to 1.18, P = 0.0002). In addition, VLCKD significantly increased the abundance of Akkermansia ( SMD : 1.76, 95% CI : 0.48 to 3.03, P = 0.0069) and the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio ( SMD : 1.01, 95% CI : 0.67 to 1.34, P < 0.0001), while significantly reducing the probiotic genus Bifidobacterium ( SMD : −1.23, 95% CI : −1.81 to −0.64, P < 0.0001). Subgroup analyses indicated that the increase in Shannon index was more pronounced in participants with BMI ≤ 30 kg/m² and age >30 years. Akkermansia showed a greater increase in those with BMI 30–35 kg/m², age >40 years, and intervention duration ≤6 weeks. Conversely, Bifidobacterium abundance declined significantly in individuals with BMI 30–35 kg/m², age >40 years, and within an intervention period ≤12 weeks. Conclusion VLCKD appears to be a promising dietary intervention for modulating gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. However, its bidirectional effects on microbial ecology warrant caution. Future studies should further investigate its long-term safety and explore personalized strategies for microbiota-targeted interventions. KEYWORDS: Very-low-calorie ketogenic diet, obesity, gut microbiota, meta-analysis, systematic review Graphical abstract status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 Jul 10; Accepted 2025 Sep 19; Collection date 2025. 1. Introduction In recent years, the global obesity crisis has become increasingly severe. According to data released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2024, over one billion individuals worldwide are classified as obese. 1 Obesity represents a state of low-grade chronic inflammation 2 and is closely associated with numerous chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, certain types of cancer, and mental disorders, substantially increasing the global disease burden. 3 Among the various intervention strategies for obesity, dietary control and physical activity are widely recognized as the most common, safe, and effective methods, especially in the context of long-term weight management. 4 Compared with single-modality interventions, the combination of scientifically guided nutrition and regular physical exercise is more effective in regulating energy intake and expenditure, improving metabolic indicators, and reducing both body fat and the risk of associated complications. 5 The ketogenic diet (KD), a dietary approach that has attracted considerable attention in recent years, is widely adopted by individuals aiming for rapid weight loss due to its potential benefits in fat reduction and metabolic improvement. 6 However, several studies have indicated that the classical KD may pose risks to renal function, endocrine regulation, and lipid metabolism, potentially promoting atherosclerosis and triggering health concerns such as “keto flu.” These risks have raised frequent clinical concerns. 6–8 With continued advances in dietary and nutritional research, the classical KD has undergone notable refinements. The very-low-calorie ketogenic diet (VLCKD) has emerged as a more structured and controllable variant of the ketogenic approach and is now regarded as a safer and more efficient dietary strategy for weight reduction. 9 VLCKD is typically characterized by a total daily caloric intake of less than 800 kcal, including fewer than 50 grams of carbohydrates per day (approximately 13% of total energy), protein intake of 1–1.5 g/kg body weight (about 44%), and fat accounting for around 43% of total energy. This strict carbohydrate restriction drives a metabolic shift from glucose to ketone bodies ( β -hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, and acetone) as the body’s primary energy source. 10 Such a shift effectively promotes fat oxidation and ketogenesis, thereby contributing to rapid reductions in body fat, improved insulin sensitivity, and better glycemic control in the short term. 11 Simultaneously, increased levels of ketone bodies have been associated with enhanced anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity, immune regulation, gut motility and barrier function, cellular growth and differentiation, mineral absorption, and the prevention of distal ulcers, Crohn’s disease, and colorectal cancer. 9 However, the gut microbiota (GM), a critical “invisible organ” involved in human metabolism, immunity, and energy regulation, is influenced by a wide range of factors, including genetics, age, environment, diet, and lifestyle. 12 , 13 A substantial body of research has demonstrated that gut dysbiosis is closely linked to metabolic disorders such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. 14–16 Among these influencing factors, diet is considered the most important external modulator of the gut microbial ecosystem, capable of rapidly altering microbial diversity, metabolite production, and host inflammatory responses. 17 Although existing studies have shown that VLCKD exerts beneficial effects on weight control, insulin resistance, and lipid metabolism, 18 its specific impact on the gut microbiota remains inconclusive and, in some aspects, controversial, warranting further investigation 9 ( Figure 1 ). In particular, no clear consensus has been reached regarding changes in microbial diversity, the responsiveness of key functional genera, and the mechanisms linking these alterations to metabolic improvement. Figure 1. The interaction between VLCKD and the gut microbiota. Therefore, the present study aims to systematically evaluate and meta-analyze the effects of VLCKD on the gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. This work seeks to synthesize current evidence on gut microbial changes following VLCKD intervention and to provide a more precise theoretical basis and practical guidance for nutritional strategies in obesity management. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. 19 The study protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [ID: CRD420251075467]. 2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Eligibility was assessed based on a predefined set of inclusion and exclusion criteria under the PICOS framework: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, and Study Design. Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (1) Reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, or theses; (2) Interventions that did not involve a very-low-calorie ketogenic diet (VLCKD); (3) Populations that were not obese; (4) Studies with incomplete outcome data, data that could not be extracted, or those involving interventions combined with dietary supplements, probiotics, or antibiotic treatments; (5) Animal or in vitro studies. Included studies were randomized or non-randomized crossover or parallel trials investigating the effect of VLCKD on the gut microbiota in obese populations. Additional inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Participants were obese (BMI ≥ 28 kg/m²), regardless of age, sex, or training status; (2) Interventions consisted of a very-low-calorie ketogenic diet. Where additional exercise interventions were included, details such as exercise duration, energy expenditure, or supplement use were reported; (3) The gut microbiota was assessed using metagenomic sequencing or 16S rRNA gene sequencing, with reported alpha diversity indices and relevant microbial measures, and sufficient data available for extraction; (4) Participants were adults aged >18 years; (5) Studies were published in English. 2.3. Search strategy A systematic literature search was conducted by two independent reviewers (WS and BZH) across four electronic databases—PubMed, EBSCOhost, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science—for articles published up to June 2025. A repeat search was performed in July 2025 to identify any newly published relevant studies. Search strategies were designed using Boolean logic and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) combined with free-text terms to ensure comprehensive retrieval. All search terms are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Reference lists of eligible studies and previous reviews were also manually screened to identify additional relevant literature and ensure all subject-specific keywords were captured. 2.4. Data extraction Retrieved articles were imported into EndNote X9 for de-duplication. Two independent reviewers (WS and BZH) screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment. Data were independently extracted using a standardized Excel spreadsheet. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (ZMQ). Extracted data included: authorship, publication year, country, participant age and sex, sample size, BMI, intervention type and duration, target parameters, and both primary and secondary outcome measures. Primary outcomes focused on changes in alpha and beta diversity of the gut microbiota (note: beta diversity could not be described quantitatively due to lack of available data). Secondary outcomes included changes in the relative abundance of specific bacterial taxa (e.g., Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium) and microbial ratios (e.g., Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes). For meta-analysis, means and standard deviations (SD) of outcomes before and after intervention were extracted. When only graphical data were available, numerical values were obtained using WebPlotDigitizer. Authors were contacted for raw data when necessary. 2.5. Risk of bias assessment Risk of bias in included studies was independently assessed by two reviewers (WS and BZH) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. 20 Six domains were evaluated: selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, reporting bias, and other potential sources of bias. Each domain was rated as “low risk,” “high risk,” or “unclear risk.” Disagreements were resolved through consultation with a third reviewer (LZY). 2.6. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses and figure generation were performed using R software, while study quality assessments were conducted using RevMan 5.3. Effect sizes were calculated using standardized mean differences (SMD). If studies reported standard errors, these were converted to SD using standard formulas. 21 When only medians, ranges, or interquartile ranges were reported, mean and SD were estimated using the method proposed by Wan et al. 22 A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) was applied in all comparisons. SMD was chosen to standardize effect sizes across studies with differing measurement units and sample sizes, thereby enabling comparison and synthesis of overall intervention effects. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, categorized according to the Cochrane Handbook: 0–40% may not be important; 30–60% may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50–90% may indicate substantial heterogeneity; and 75–100% suggests considerable heterogeneity. 20 In cases of high heterogeneity, subgroup analyses and meta-regression were performed to explore potential sources. The evidence of small-study effects was assessed using Egger’s regression asymmetry test, 23 and publication bias across studies was evaluated using funnel plot analysis. 3. Results A total of 28696 records were identified through electronic database searching. No additional records were identified by screening reference lists of included articles, previous systematic reviews, or other sources. After removing duplicates, 16432 studies remained for screening. Of these, 849 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 14 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Figure 2. PRISMA flow diagram of study selection process. 3.1. Study characteristics A total of 14 studies published between 2009 and 2025 were included in this review. These studies were conducted in Sweden ( n = 1), the United States ( n = 1), Italy ( n = 4), Australia ( n = 1), Spain ( n = 2), Turkey ( n = 1), Germany ( n = 1), Finland ( n = 1), and China ( n = 2). The combined sample size was 286 participants, with individual study sizes ranging from 7 participants 24 to 48 participants. 25 , 26 The average participant age ranged from 18 to 56.2 years, 25 , 27 and mean BMI ranged from 29.81 to 48.67 kg/m 2 . 28 , 29 All 14 studies reported participant sex. Two studies included only female participants, 29 , 30 while the remaining 12 studies included both male and female participants. 24–28,31–37 Most studies ( n = 9) employed 16S rRNA gene sequencing for gut microbiota analysis, 25,29–31,35 targeting different variable regions (V2–V4–V8, V3–V4, V4–V5) to assess α -diversity, β -diversity, and microbial composition changes. Five studies did not report the targeted region. 24 , 26 , 27 , 34 , 36 An overview of the included studies is presented in Table 1 . Table 1. Summary of interventions included in study. Risk of bias and publication bias The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Among the 14 studies included in the analysis, 7 employed blinded outcome assessment, and all 14 reported complete outcome data. One study was rated as having a low risk of bias, 10 studies had a moderate risk, and 3 studies were considered at high risk of bias (Supplementary Figure S1). Overall, based on risk of bias evaluation, 7 studies (50%) were considered high quality, 4 studies (28%) were of moderate quality, and 3 studies (22%) were of low quality. Funnel plot analysis and Egger’s test were conducted to assess publication bias. The funnel plot showed an approximately symmetrical distribution, suggesting a low risk of publication bias or small-study effects. 3.3. Results of meta-analysis 3.3.1. Primary outcomes The primary outcomes focused on alpha diversity measures, including Shannon index, Simpson index, OTUs, Chao1, and Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) index ( Figure 3 ). Six studies (9 effect sizes, 256 subjects) reported Shannon index data. The random-effects meta-analysis indicated that VLCKD significantly improved the Shannon index in individuals with obesity ( SMD : 0.54, 95% CI : 0.03 to 1.04, P = 0.0378), with substantial heterogeneity across studies ( I² = 71.5%). Three studies (3 effect sizes, 102 subjects) provided PD index data, and the meta-analysis showed a significant improvement ( SMD : 0.77, 95% CI : 0.36 to 1.18, P = 0.0002). Although we assessed OTUs, Chao1 and Simpson indices separately, no significant effects were detected, suggesting that VLCKD may have limited influence on the richness of rare species and the dominance structure of the gut microbiota. The significant improvement in the PD index implies that VLCKD may enhance evolutionary diversity and ecological complexity in the gut. Figure 3. Forest plot of the effects of VLCKD on gut microbiota diversity in individuals with obesity. To explore sources of high heterogeneity, we first conducted sensitivity analyses. Egger’s test and funnel plot analysis were used to assess potential publication bias ( Figure 4a ). Subsequently, subgroup analyses and meta-regression were performed to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity ( Figure 5a–c ). Subgroup analyses were stratified by BMI, age, and intervention duration (Supplementary Table S2). Results showed that age significantly moderated the intervention effect, with statistically significant between-group differences ( Pd < 0.01), indicating that age may be a key source of heterogeneity. Specifically, the effects were more pronounced in individuals aged >30 years and those with BMI ≤ 30 kg/m² ( P < 0.05). Meta-regression revealed a positive regression slope with age, suggesting that intervention efficacy may increase with age. Figure 4. Funnel plot of the effects of VLCKD on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. (a) (the gut microbiota diversity), (b) (the abundance of key gut microbial taxa). Figure 5. Meta-regression of the effects of VLCKD on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity. 3.3.2. Secondary outcomes For Akkermansia, four studies (5 effect sizes, 108 subjects) showed that VLCKD significantly increased its abundance under a random-effects model ( SMD : 1.76, 95% CI : 0.48 to 3.03, P = 0.0069), with high heterogeneity ( I² = 85.8%). Regarding Bifidobacterium, meta-analysis indicated a significant negative effect ( SMD : -1.23, 95% CI : -1.81 to -0.64, P < 0.0001), suggesting that VLCKD may markedly reduce this key probiotic, potentially posing health risks—a point discussed further in the discussion section. As for the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio, VLCKD significantly increased the ratio ( SMD : 1.01, 95% CI : 0.67 to 1.34, P < 0.0001), indicating stability and consistency in the observed direction of change ( Figure 6 ). Figure 6. Forest plot of the effects of VLCKD on the abundance of key gut microbial taxa in individuals with obesity. To further investigate sources of heterogeneity, sensitivity analysis was performed. Egger’s test and funnel plot analysis were used to assess publication bias ( Figure 4b ). Subgroup analyses (Supplementary Table S3) and meta-regression ( Figure 5d–f ) were conducted using BMI, age, and intervention duration as moderator variables. For Akkermansia, BMI significantly moderated the effect of the intervention. The most notable effects were observed in individuals with BMI between 30–35 kg/m². Although effects were also significant in those with BMI > 40 kg/m², the limited number of studies in this subgroup may reduce the robustness of the evidence; thus, this result was excluded from the main conclusions. Regarding age, individuals over 40 years exhibited significant increases in Akkermansia abundance. In terms of intervention duration, only interventions ≤ 6 weeks showed significant effects in subgroup analyses. For Bifidobacterium, subgroup analyses (Supplementary Table S4) indicated a significant negative effect in individuals with BMI between 30–35 kg/m², suggesting stronger suppression of this probiotic in this weight category. Similarly, significant reductions were observed in those with BMI > 40 kg/m²; however, due to the small number of studies, this finding was not considered robust. In age-stratified analysis, significant negative changes were observed in participants older than 40 years, implying that age may be an important moderator of the intervention effect. However, in the 40–50 year subgroup, only one study was included, limiting the reliability of the finding. With respect to intervention duration, significant effects were observed in both ≤ 6-week and 6–12-week subgroups. Meta-regression revealed a mildly positive trend with age, suggesting that while the intervention effect may improve with increasing mean age, the enhancement remains modest. 4. Discussion This meta-analysis aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of VLCKD on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity, and to further explore potential moderating factors. The main findings indicate that VLCKD interventions significantly enhanced gut microbial diversity, as evidenced by notable increases in the Shannon index and Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity (PD) index. Additionally, VLCKD significantly increased the abundance of Akkermansia, while reducing the abundance of Bifidobacterium, along with an elevated Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio. These results suggest that VLCKD exerts bidirectional effects on microbial structure. Our findings support the growing view that VLCKD can effectively modulate the gut microbial ecosystem and lead to short-term improvements in microbial diversity. However, the significant reduction in Bifidobacterium may indicate potential risks to gut barrier integrity and probiotic balance. This observation has important implications for long-term VLCKD interventions in obese populations. It highlights the need to monitor probiotic stability and gut health during implementation, and suggests that individualized supplementation strategies—such as dietary fiber or probiotics—may be necessary to maintain microbial stability and safety. 38 4.1. Changes in gut microbiota diversity indices Gut microbial diversity, particularly alpha diversity, is a key indicator of intestinal health and has been closely associated with the development of various diseases. According to a review by Li et al., 39 gut microbial diversity may serve as a potential biomarker for the early prediction of multiple diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and multiple sclerosis. Higher microbial diversity is typically linked to greater intestinal resilience, enhanced immune function, and reduced levels of inflammation. 40 Our meta-analysis demonstrated that VLCKD significantly increased alpha diversity indices in individuals with obesity, including the Shannon index and PD index. These metrics reflect improvements in gut health across different dimensions: the Shannon index captures species evenness, and PD index reflects phylogenetic and evolutionary complexity. In contrast, the Observed OTU, Simpson and Chao1 indices did not show significant changes, likely due to their lower sensitivity to changes in dominant or low-abundance taxa. VLCKD alters the ratio of dietary fats to carbohydrates, which may substantially shift the availability of microbial substrates in the gut. This shift could favor the growth of fat-tolerant and mucin-degrading bacteria, thereby driving changes in microbiota structure and diversity. 41 , 42 It is worth noting that VLCKD appears to primarily affect common or dominant microbial taxa, while its influence on low-abundance or rare species is limited. This may partly explain why some diversity indices did not reach statistical significance. 43 , 44 Moreover, subgroup analyses showed that VLCKD had a more pronounced effect on microbial diversity among individuals aged over 30 years. This may be due to age-related microbial dysbiosis and the decline of gut microbial diversity observed in older adults. Aging is associated with greater gut microbial instability, which may render the microbiota more responsive to dietary interventions. Therefore, VLCKD may induce more substantial structural shifts in populations with baseline dysbiosis, particularly in older individuals. 45 , 46 Additionally, the findings revealed that VLCKD had stronger effects in individuals with BMI ≤ 30 kg/m², suggesting that the gut microbiota of mildly obese individuals may be more responsive to dietary interventions. This may be explained by the greater ecological plasticity of the microbiome in individuals with Class I obesity or lower BMI. Conversely, with higher BMI, the gut microbiota often exhibits dominant taxa fixation, resulting in reduced plasticity to dietary interventions and decreased sensitivity to their effects. 47 , 48 Specifically, these dominant taxa have been reported in some studies to play a central role in metabolic pathways related to high-efficiency energy utilization, such as starch degradation, aromatic amino acid biosynthesis, and nucleotide biosynthesis, thereby establishing a relatively fixed metabolic pattern that limits microbiota changes induced by dietary interventions. 27 , 49 Moreover, individuals with higher BMI frequently present with impaired intestinal barrier function, increased intestinal permeability, and metabolic endotoxemia. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) can activate the TLR4–NF-κB signaling pathway, triggering sustained elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which not only exacerbates metabolic dysregulation but also inhibits the colonization and expansion of beneficial microbes such as Bifidobacterium and butyrate-producing bacteria. 50 These results indicate that the microbial modulatory effects of VLCKD may vary across individuals. However, BMI has consistently been identified as a key mediator in the relationship between dietary intervention and microbiome composition. 51 Future research with larger sample sizes and more diverse populations is warranted to validate these findings. 4.2. Alterations in characteristic gut microbiota Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes are the two dominant bacterial phyla in the adult gut microbiota, together accounting for approximately 90% of its composition. 52 F/B ratio reflects the relative abundance between these two major phyla and is often used as an indicator of microbial balance. A higher F/B ratio has been associated with obesity, metabolic dysfunction, and gut dysbiosis. 53 , 54 In the present study, VLCKD intervention did not significantly alter the individual abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes in obese individuals; however, a significant increase was observed in the F/B ratio. This may be due to the F/B ratio’s heightened sensitivity to subtle community shifts, especially in the context of obesity and intestinal inflammation. In contrast, changes in single phyla may be masked by inter-individual variability or sequencing methodology. 52 , 55 Firmicutes dominate in lipid metabolism and can efficiently utilize fat-derived metabolites, leading to their rapid expansion in high-fat dietary environments. On the other hand, Bacteroidetes specialize in metabolizing dietary fiber and complex carbohydrates. The VLCKD’s severe carbohydrate restriction reduces substrate availability for Bacteroidetes, potentially contributing to their relative decline. Prior research has suggested that the F/B ratio is more statistically sensitive than single phyla abundance in detecting dietary intervention effects, and more closely linked to obesity- and metabolism-related phenotypes. 56 Traditionally, an elevated F/B ratio is associated with increased energy harvest efficiency, enhanced fat storage, and low-grade chronic inflammation—features characteristic of obesity, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes. However, under VLCKD intervention, an increase in the F/B ratio may not necessarily reflect pathological dysbiosis. Rather, it may indicate an adaptive microbial restructuring in response to the dietary regimen. This is consistent with findings from Tanca et al., 41 who observed that VLCKD induced short-term increases in both F/B ratio and Akkermansia abundance, suggesting that the observed microbial shifts likely reflect a favorable adaptive response. Akkermansia is widely recognized for its anti-obesity, anti-inflammatory, and gut barrier-enhancing properties, and is considered one of the key taxa responsive to ketogenic diets. 57 VLCKD alters intestinal substrate availability by reducing carbohydrates, thereby increasing reliance on mucus—the primary substrate for Akkermansia—which promotes its proliferation. 58 Subgroup analysis revealed a significant effect in individuals with BMI between 30–35 kg/m². This may be attributed to greater ecological plasticity in this group, where the microbiota remains more modifiable and responsive to dietary shifts. 47 Additionally, Akkermansia appears to exert more pronounced anti-obesity effects in individuals over 40 years of age. Its abundance is inversely associated with obesity risk, suggesting that older individuals, who typically exhibit greater baseline dysbiosis and reduced microbial diversity, are more sensitive to VLCKD-induced microbial shifts. 59 As aging is associated with decreased gut diversity, weakened barrier function, and greater susceptibility to dysbiosis, Akkermansia may more easily occupy ecological niches during intervention. 58 During short-term dietary interventions, the gut microbiota is highly sensitive to acute dietary changes, enabling rapid expansion of Akkermansia within days. This bacterium relies on host-secreted mucin polysaccharides as its primary carbon source and is extremely sensitive to changes in substrate availability and mucin layer metabolism. Dietary patterns characterized by a marked restriction of carbohydrates and an increased proportion of lipids can accelerate mucin layer metabolism in the gut, leading to a rapid rise in Akkermansia abundance over a short period, accompanied by enhanced expression of functional proteins related to stress responses and neurotransmitter metabolism (such as γ -aminobutyric acid synthase). 41 , 60 However, during long-term ketogenic dieting, the gut micro-ecology gradually undergoes compensatory restructuring. Other commensal species, through metabolic interactions and resource competition, suppress the over-proliferation of a single species, while host immunity and mucin layer renewal rates may also be feedback-regulated, causing Akkermansia abundance to gradually decline. In addition, long-term interventions may lead to dietary fatigue and reduced compliance, resulting in Akkermansia abundance returning toward a new steady state. 58 , 61 , 62 Further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify these dynamic patterns and their clinical significance. Bifidobacterium is a well-established core probiotic that contributes to host health by producing short-chain fatty acids (e.g., acetate), modulating immune responses, enhancing intestinal barrier integrity, and maintaining microbial homeostasis. 63 , 64 A decline in Bifidobacterium abundance has been linked to increased risk of several chronic diseases, including allergic asthma, colitis, type 2 diabetes, and depression. 38 , 65 , 66 SCFAs are key metabolites produced by the fermentation of dietary fibers by the gut microbiota. They serve as an important energy source and exert regulatory effects on metabolism, immunity, and the nervous system through the activation of G-protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) and the inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs), thereby contributing to energy supply, immune modulation, and metabolic improvement. 67 , 68 Bifidobacterium is recognized as an important producer of SCFAs. 69 Salazar et al. 70 reported that in obese women, an increase in Bifidobacterium was accompanied by a reduction in SCFA levels. In contrast, Canfora et al. 71 found that in overweight or obese men and women with prediabetes, higher Bifidobacterium abundance was not associated with significant alterations in SCFA concentrations. Similarly, Solito et al. 72 demonstrated that in obese adolescents, supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve BR03 and B632 for 8 weeks improved insulin sensitivity, yet SCFA levels, especially acetate, did not significantly increase. Collectively, these findings highlight the lack of consistency across studies investigating obese populations of different ages, sexes, and comorbidity status. Future research should focus on these issues to achieve greater consensus. Our subgroup analysis revealed that VLCKD significantly reduced Bifidobacterium abundance, with the most pronounced effect observed in individuals with BMI 30–35 kg/m². This may represent a critical “window of plasticity,” during which the gut microbiota remains modifiable and responsive to dietary stressors. 73 The severe carbohydrate restriction and high-fat nature of VLCKD markedly reduce the availability of fermentable fibers and oligosaccharides—substrates essential for Bifidobacterium—thus favoring the dominance of fat-tolerant microbial communities and suppressing Bifidobacterium growth. 74 Additionally, subgroup analyses by age and intervention duration showed that Bifidobacterium significantly declined in individuals aged >40 years undergoing VLCKD for 0–12 weeks. This may be due to age-related changes in the gut environment, including decreased gastric acid secretion, reduced digestive enzyme activity, and slower intestinal transit, all of which impair probiotic colonization, particularly for Bifidobacterium. 75 , 76 In the short term, the strict restriction of carbohydrates and fermentable fibers in the diet reduces the substrates available for Bifidobacterium. 77 At the same time, acute VLCKD induces rapid ketogenesis, elevating ketones such as β -hydroxybutyrate. High concentrations of ketones may indirectly inhibit certain anaerobic probiotics by reducing gut pH or destabilizing bacterial membranes. 17 Notably, ketone bodies selectively inhibited bifidobacterial growth. 74 In contrast, during long-term interventions, compensatory remodeling of the gut ecosystem appears to occur. Evidence suggests that the microbial community may partially recover or stabilize, likely due to cross-feeding interactions among microbes and host feedback mechanisms regulating mucosal barrier renewal and immune tolerance. 35 However, cautious evaluation is required regarding the long-term nutritional safety and potential risks to gut health. 78 , 79 In summary, VLCKD exerts dual effects on characteristic gut microbial taxa in individuals with obesity: On the one hand, the increase in Akkermansia reflects an adaptive and potentially beneficial microbial response to the dietary shift. On the other hand, the marked suppression of Bifidobacterium raises concerns about gut barrier integrity and chronic disease risk. These findings underscore the need for careful monitoring and individualized dietary planning during VLCKD interventions. Future large-scale, long-duration randomized controlled trials are warranted to further elucidate the underlying microbial mechanisms and evaluate the long-term safety of VLCKD across diverse populations. 4.3. Limitations of the study First, the number of included studies for certain outcomes was limited. Although this review adhered strictly to systematic review procedures, the current body of research on the effects of VLCKD on gut microbiota in individuals with obesity remains sparse. Some microbial outcomes were derived from only 3 to 5 studies, potentially compromising the precision and robustness of effect size estimates. For example, When conducting subgroup analysis, only the Shannon index, Akkermansia, and Bifidobacterium were analyzed. Meanwhile, when analyzing Bifidobacterium, the levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) should be reported simultaneously, as there is a relevant association between them; however, due to a lack of eligible studies (fewer than three), meta-analysis of SCFA data could not be conducted. Second, there was inconsistency in microbial sequencing regions and analytical approaches across studies. Although most studies used 16S rRNA sequencing, the choice of hypervariable regions (e.g., V3–V4, V4, V4–V5) and data processing platforms varied considerably, which may have affected the comparability of microbial abundance and diversity indices, introducing methodological bias. Third, despite being uniformly labeled as "VLCKD," the intervention protocols varied substantially in total caloric intake, fat-to-protein ratios, use of medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) or exogenous ketones, and dietary supplementation. These differences may have altered the gut substrate environment and contributed to heterogeneity in microbiota responses and effect estimates. Finally, the included studies were conducted across diverse geographic regions (including Europe, North America, and Asia), where differences in genetic background, dietary habits, gut microbial baseline composition, and lifestyle factors could systematically influence individual responses to VLCKD. These contextual factors may limit the generalizability of the findings. 5. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates that VLCKD can significantly enhance gut microbial diversity in individuals with obesity, as evidenced by increases in the Shannon index and PD index. Additionally, VLCKD significantly increased Akkermansia abundance and the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio, while concurrently reducing the abundance of Bifidobacterium. These findings highlight the dual ecological effects of VLCKD—potentially beneficial modulation of microbial diversity, but also possible risks of dysbiosis due to probiotic depletion. Subgroup analyses revealed that improvements in microbial diversity (Shannon index) were more pronounced in individuals aged >30 years and with BMI > 30 kg/m². The most notable increases in Akkermansia were observed in individuals with BMI between 30–35 kg/m², aged over 40, and within intervention periods ≤ 6 weeks. In contrast, reductions in Bifidobacterium were most significant in those with BMI 30–35 kg/m², age >40 years, and intervention durations ≤ 12 weeks. Future research should place greater emphasis on preserving core probiotics, exploring the potential of co-administration with probiotics, and assessing the long-term ecological safety of VLCKD. Large-scale, high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to further validate these findings and guide safe, personalized dietary interventions for obesity management. documents.title: Risk prediction model for post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography pancreatitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography pancreatitis (PEP) is the most common and clinically significant complication of ERCP, with an incidence of 3.5-9.7% in general populations and up to 14.7% in high-risk groups, leading to considerable morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Although numerous multivariable prediction models have been developed, their predictor sets, methodological rigor, and clinical applicability remain highly variable.
METHOD: We conducted a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis, prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024556967). Nine databases were searched to June 1, 2024, for studies developing or validating multivariable PEP risk prediction models. Data on study/model characteristics, predictors, and performance metrics were extracted. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST, and study quality with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled (i) PEP incidence, (ii) associations of individual predictors, and (iii) overall model performance.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies (26 models; n = 38,016) published from 2002-2024 were included, predominantly retrospective cohorts from East Asia (n = 16). The pooled PEP incidence was 8.48% (95% CI: 6.90-10.39%; I² = 96.4%), highest in East Asia and retrospective cohorts. Strongest predictors included pancreatic duct cannulation (OR=3.50), pancreatic injection (OR=3.50), previous pancreatitis (OR=3.32), and pancreatic guidewire use (OR=2.63); additional consistent factors were female sex, difficult cannulation, elevated bilirubin, low albumin, choledocholithiasis, and prolonged procedure time. The pooled odds ratio for model performance was 0.81 (95% CI: 0.78-0.84; I² = 83.5%), with AUCs ranging 0.560-0.915, though calibration was infrequently reported (38%) and external validation undertaken in only 46%. PROBAST indicated high overall risk of bias, chiefly in the analysis (92%) and participants (100%) domains.
CONCLUSION: Current PEP prediction models generally demonstrate moderate-to-high discrimination but are limited by suboptimal calibration, inadequate external validation, and methodological heterogeneity. Future research should adhere to TRIPOD guidelines, employ multicenter large-sample designs, retain continuous predictors, address missing data with robust imputation methods, and conduct comprehensive temporal, geographic, and domain-specific validation. Integration of artificial intelligence/machine learning with conventional modeling and embedding validated tools into clinical workflows may enhance predictive accuracy and real-world utility.

Introduction Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is widely utilized for diagnosing and treating biliopancreatic diseases [ 1 , 2 ]. Compared with traditional surgery, ERCP offers several advantages, including reduced surgical trauma, faster postoperative recovery, shorter treatment durations, and briefer hospital stays [ 3 ]. However, as an invasive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure, ERCP carries inherent risks, particularly procedure-related complications. Among these, post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) is the most common, with an incidence of 3.5–9.7% in the general population and up to 14.7% in high-risk patients. The mortality rate associated with PEP ranges from 0.1% to 0.7% [ 2 , 4 , 5 ]. While mild cases may simply prolong hospitalization, severe PEP can result in pancreatic necrosis, multiple organ failure, or even death [ 6 , 7 ]. These adverse outcomes not only compromise procedural success and patient prognosis but also impose substantial economic burdens on patients, healthcare systems, and society. To mitigate these consequences, accurate identification of patients at high risk of PEP is essential. Risk prediction models offer clinicians a tool to estimate individual PEP risk and tailor preventive strategies accordingly. By stratifying patients according to predicted risk, unnecessary admissions can be reduced, preventive measures can be targeted, and overall healthcare costs can be lowered-ultimately improving patient quality of life. In recent years, multiple PEP risk prediction models have been developed using different predictors, statistical methods, and validation strategies. However, their methodological quality, external validity, and clinical applicability vary considerably. Moreover, the predictors incorporated into these models differ substantially across studies, reflecting variations in patient populations, procedural techniques, and study designs. While such heterogeneity is inevitable, it raises important questions: which predictors show consistent, clinically meaningful associations with PEP? How well do existing models perform overall? And what is the true incidence of PEP in the populations studied? A systematic review and meta-analysis provides a rigorous approach to address these questions. By synthesizing available evidence, such an approach can: (i) quantify the pooled incidence of PEP across diverse populations; (ii) identify predictors with consistent, statistically significant associations with PEP; (iii) evaluate the overall predictive performance of existing models, considering both discrimination and calibration; (iv) assess the methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies. Therefore, the aim of this study was to systematically review and meta-analyze existing PEP risk prediction models, with a focus on their predictive performance, methodological rigor, and clinical applicability. Through this synthesis, we aim to provide robust, evidence-based recommendations to guide both clinical decision-making and future model development. Methods This study was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024556967) and conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. For detailed information, please refer to S1 Table . Search strategy We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, The Cochrane Library, Embase, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Database, China Science and Technology Journal Database (VIP), and SinoMed from inception to June 1, 2024. The detailed search strategies for each database are provided in S2 and S3 Tables . Inclusion and exclusion criteria The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) studies involving patients underwent ERCP; (ii) observational study design (cohort or case-control), or interventional studies that developed or validated a PEP prediction model; (iii) reported outcome of post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP); and (iv) inclusion of a multivariable prediction model. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) studies that only assessed risk factors without constructing a prediction model; (ii) studies without available full text; (iii) gray literature, including conference abstracts and agency reports; (iv) duplicate publications; and (v) studies not written in English or Chinese. Study selection and screening Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts according to the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. Data extraction Data were extracted into a standardized form and categorized as: (i) study characteristics: first author, year, country/region, research design, data source, study period, and PEP diagnostic criteria; (ii) model characteristics: sample size, outcome event rate, events per variable (EPV), model development method, variable selection method, handling of missing data, and treatment of continuous variables; (iii) model performance: discrimination (e.g., AUC/C-statistic), calibration, type of validation (internal vs. external), and model presentation format; and (iv) predictors: number and type of candidate variables and final predictors included in the model. Quality assessment The methodological quality and applicability were assessed using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) [ 8 ]. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was employed to assess the quality of observational studies [ 9 ]. Two reviewers (YM. & QL.) independently rated the certainty of evidence using the GRADE system (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) [ 10 ], with disagreements resolved through discussion. Data synthesis and statistic analysis We performed three complementary meta-analyses: 1 Pooled incidence of PEP Extracted incidence data (events/total) from each study. Proportions were pooled using a random-effects model with logit transformation to stabilize variances. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran’s Q test and quantified by I²; thresholds of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicated low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Subgroup analyses were planned by geographic region, study design, diagnostic definition and validation method. 2 Pooled associations of individual predictors For predictors reported in ≥3 studies, effect estimates (odds ratios [OR], relative risks [RR], hazard ratios [HR]) and 95% CIs were extracted; RRs and HRs were converted to ORs if necessary. Random-effects meta-analyses (restricted maximum likelihood estimator) were performed separately for each predictor. Heterogeneity and publication bias (Egger’s test, funnel plots) were evaluated when ≥10 studies were available. Sensitivity analyses excluded high risk-of-bias studies or those with small sample sizes (<100 participants). 3 Pooled predictive performance of models Discrimination was quantified by the AUC (C-statistic). AUC values were pooled on the logit scale and back-transformed for presentation. Priority was given to externally validated results; internal validation was used if external validation was unavailable. All analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the meta, metafor, and mada packages. Two-tailed p-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Results Study selection Our search identified 962 records, with 57 duplicates removed. After screening 905 articles, 783 were excluded as irrelevant. An further 98 full-text articles were excluded for the following reasons: conference abstracts (n = 26), no risk prediction model (n = 36), fewer than two predictors (n = 2), abstract only (n = 23), and not primary literature (n = 11). In total, 24 studies [ 11 – 34 ] reporting 26 PEP prediction models met the inclusion criteria ( Fig 1 ). 10.1371/journal.pone.0332378.g001 Fig 1 Search results and study selection. Study characteristics The 24 studies were published between 2002 and 2024, with 20 published in the last five years. Sixteen studies were conducted in China, four in Japan, two in the United States, one in Korea, and one in Italy. Study designs comprised 20 retrospective cohort, two prospective cohort, one cross-sectional study, and one case-control study. Diagnostic criteria for PEP varied: 13 studies used the Cotton Expert Consensus Criteria [ 35 ], nine the Atlanta Criteria [ 36 ], one the Chinese MDT Consensus [ 37 ], and one the ASGE criteria [ 38 ]. Predictive performance of models Our systematic review and meta-analysis included 13 studies evaluating risk prediction models for ERCP pancreatitis. The pooled analysis demonstrated that these prediction models had significant predictive value, with an overall odds ratio (OR) of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.77–0.84) using a random-effects model. Considerable heterogeneity was observed among studies (I 2 = 82.0%, τ² = 0.0041, p < 0.0001), suggesting substantial variation in model performance across different settings ( Fig 4 ). 10.1371/journal.pone.0332378.g004 Fig 4 Forest plot of the meta-analysis of pooled AUC estimates for predictive models performance. Subgroup analyses Dataset type. Analysis stratified by dataset type (development vs. validation groups) revealed no significant difference between subgroups (χ²₁ = 1.44, p = 0.2303). The development group showed an OR of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72–0.85, I 2 = 89.8%), while the validation group demonstrated an OR of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.78–0.87, I 2 = 47.3%) ( S7A Fig ). Diagnostic criteria. Subgroup analysis by diagnostic criteria (Atlanta classification, Chinese consensus, and Cotton criterion) showed no statistically significant differences between subgroups (χ²₂ = 4.57, p = 0.1020). Models using Atlanta classification had an OR of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.76–0.86, I 2 = 67.2%), while those using Cotton criterion showed an OR of 0.77 (95% CI: 0.70–0.85, I 2 = 71.9%) ( S7B Fig ). Study design. Significant differences were observed across study designs (χ²₃ = 45.21, p < 0.0001). Retrospective cohort studies (OR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.80–0.85, I 2 = 34.3%) constituted the majority of included studies. Cross-sectional studies showed higher predictive values (OR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.70–1.00, single study), while prospective cohort studies demonstrated lower values (OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.64–0.76) ( S7C Fig ). Models with both internal and external validation showed the most consistent results (OR = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.85–0.88, I 2 = 0%), differing significantly from those with internal validation only (OR = 0.79, 95% CI: 0.72–0.85, I 2 = 72.5%) or no validation (OR = 0.80, 95% CI: 0.73–0.87, I 2 = 90.5%) (χ²₂ = 14.64, p = 0.0007) ( S7D Fig ). Geographic region. Significant regional variations were observed (χ²₂ = 46.69, p < 0.0001). East Asian studies predominated (OR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.80–0.85, I 2 = 27.2%), while European (OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.64–0.76) and North American studies (OR = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.68–0.74) showed lower predictive values ( S7E Fig ).
